question: Which major salivary gland contributes most significantly to total resting salivary flow?
explanation: The submandibular glands produce the majority of unstimulated, resting saliva in the oral cavity. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h1)

question: Why is the epithelium of the hard palate keratinized while the floor of the mouth is non-keratinized?

options.A: Non-keratinized tissue increases the absorption of salivary digestive enzymes
options.B: Non-keratinized tissue is necessary for rapid taste bud regeneration
options.C: Keratinization provides resistance to frictional forces from mastication
options.D: Keratinized cells prevent the downward flow of saliva into the throat

explanation: Areas exposed to heavy mechanical friction during chewing develop keratinized stratified squamous epithelium for structural protection. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h1)

question: What characteristic clinical finding differentiates oral candidiasis from milk curds in the mouth?

options.A: Milk curds are firmly attached to the underlying palate
options.B: Candidiasis lesions exclusively appear on the dorsal surface of the tongue
options.C: Candidiasis plaques leave a bleeding base when scraped
options.D: Milk curds cause intense localized burning pain and mucosal erythema

explanation: Scraping candida plaques removes the pseudomembrane and typically exposes an erythematous, bleeding mucosal surface underneath. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h2)

question: A patient undergoing cancer chemotherapy develops severe generalized painful ulcers throughout the oral cavity. What is the standard clinical term for this presentation?
explanation: Stomatitis describes an inflammatory reaction affecting the oral mucosa, frequently seen as a complication of cytotoxic chemotherapy. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which premalignant oral lesion carries the highest statistical risk for malignant transformation into squamous cell carcinoma?
explanation: Erythroplakia presents as a red patch and possesses a substantially higher rate of dysplasia and progression to cancer compared to white lesions. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h3)

question: A 55-year-old man who smokes cigarettes and drinks alcohol daily presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the lateral border of his tongue that has persisted for two months. What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic action?

options.A: Reassuring the patient and scheduling follow-up in six months
options.B: Performing a tissue biopsy for histological examination
options.C: Prescribing a two-week course of topical antifungal oral gel
options.D: Initiating broad-spectrum systemic intravenous antibiotic therapy

explanation: Any persistent, non-healing oral lesion in a high-risk patient requires a tissue biopsy to rule out squamous cell carcinoma. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h3)

question: What is the definitive diagnostic procedure used to confirm squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity?
explanation: Histological examination of a tissue sample obtained via biopsy provides definitive confirmation of malignancy. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which component is essential when documenting an abnormal lesion found during a routine nursing oral assessment?

options.A: The patient's exact blood pressure at the time of discovery
options.B: Precise anatomical location, size, and color characteristics
options.C: Family history of chronic systemic cardiovascular disease
options.D: The brand of toothpaste the patient routinely uses daily

explanation: Accurate baseline documentation of a lesion's physical dimensions and appearance is vital for tracking progression or response to therapy. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h4)

question: Which medication is classified as an antifungal agent commonly used to treat oral candidiasis?
explanation: Nystatin is a standard topical antifungal agent used to manage fungal overgrowth in the oral cavity. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why is viscous lidocaine prescribed for patients experiencing severe painful stomatitis?

options.A: To permanently eradicate the underlying viral infection causing the ulcers
options.B: To prevent secondary fungal colonization on the denuded mucosa
options.C: To provide temporary local anesthesia so the patient can tolerate eating
options.D: To promote the rapid healing and closure of deep mucosal craters

explanation: Viscous lidocaine numbs the oral mucosa, alleviating pain sufficiently to allow patients to ingest food and fluids. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary immediate postoperative priority for a patient recovering from radical oral surgery?
explanation: Airway compromise due to surgical swelling, bleeding, or secretions is the most critical immediate postoperative risk. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h6)

question: What clinical sign indicates compromised arterial blood flow to a newly grafted tissue flap in the oral cavity?
explanation: Inadequate arterial inflow results in pallor and coolness, whereas venous congestion presents as dusky, purple discoloration. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h6)

question: Which dietary modification is most appropriate for a patient experiencing severe painful oral ulcerations?

options.B: Providing hot, highly spiced, and acidic meals
options.C: Encouraging hard, crunchy raw vegetable snacks
options.D: Serving soft, bland, and lukewarm foods

explanation: Soft, bland, and lukewarm foods minimize physical and chemical irritation to compromised mucosal surfaces. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h7)

question: What is NOT a primary lifestyle modification nurses should teach patients to prevent oral cancer? [FRAME]

options.B: Increasing dietary intake of refined sugars

explanation: Refined sugars contribute to dental caries but are not a recognized primary target for preventing oral squamous cell carcinoma. [learn more](GNS213_U3_T4#GNS213_U3_T4_h7)
